World Lab is a horizontal map/timeline-style editor for World Elements: biome regions and transitions, puzzle instances, bespoke dressing, semantic dressing groups, terraforming machines/landmarks and later story/camera/audio/VFX/checkpoint elements.

It is not a separate level file. It is a second editing interface over the same authoritative placement data used by the game/editor, allowing scene placements to appear as World Lab markers and World Lab changes to appear immediately back in the game.

children.title: Concept Lab
children.body:
**Purpose:** keep visual development inside the SideScroll project instead of scattered across chat history.

Concept Lab should organise images by World / Biome / Terraform Machine / Character / Location. Each concept record should keep the image, source prompt/brief, notes, status, date/version and links to related Design Lab entries.

Support several iterations with states such as **Exploration / Shortlisted / Approved Direction / Superseded**. Initial implementation should focus on importing and browsing concepts; integrated generation can come later and must not expose an AI API key in the static GitHub Pages client.

The initial visual-development brief is documented in **Concept Development & Image Brief** and mirrored in repository file `CONCEPT_ART_BRIEF.md` for handoff to image-generation sessions.

children.title: Content Data to Formalise
children.body:
- Chapter manifests and ordered section definitions.
- Puzzle template definitions plus per-instance overrides/state.
- Asset metadata: visual layout, collision, behaviour and named states.
- Thought/story trigger data and narrative flags.
- Audio/VFX emitter definitions.
- Checkpoint and save-state schema.

sections.title: Project Workflow
sections.body:
This page is the source-of-truth for how SideScroll moves between ChatGPT, the iPhone and GitHub. The goal is to keep development **phone-first**, minimise unnecessary file transfer, preserve simple rollback points and make each change easy to understand.

## Principle
GitHub holds the live project. ChatGPT changes only the files required for a task. Normal development uses small patch ZIPs; periodic full ZIPs remain known-good snapshots.

## Current baseline
The current full project baseline for this workflow test is **SideScroll v1.0.62**.

children.title: READ FIRST — Assistant / Fresh-Chat Working Rules
children.body:
This entry is written **for any future ChatGPT/Codex-style session working on SideScroll**. When a SideScroll ZIP is supplied in a fresh conversation, read the repository `README.md` and this entry before editing files. Treat these rules as the default project contract unless the user explicitly changes them.

## 1. Phone-first workflow is a design constraint
The project is primarily developed, uploaded to GitHub and tested from an iPhone. Prefer solutions that preserve that workflow. Do not introduce a desktop-only build step, package manager or toolchain unless there is a clear need and the user agrees.

## 2. Default delivery = changed-files-only PATCH ZIP
Normal iterative work should return a flat **PATCH ZIP containing only changed/new project files plus an updated `README.md`**.

Do not include unchanged textures, audio, atlases, HTML pages or other large assets simply because they exist in the project.

Create a FULL ZIP only when the user asks for one or at a meaningful safety/milestone point such as a large structural refactor, new tool/lab, major data-schema change, substantial asset pack, vertical slice or known-good checkpoint.

## 3. README is mandatory in every patch
Every patch must include an updated `README.md` stating:
- required base/current project state;
- changed files;
- added files;
- intentional deletions/renames;
- what the patch changes;
- what the user should test;
- any cache/reopen instructions.

A file missing from a patch means **unchanged**, never “delete it”. Deletions must be stated explicitly.

## 4. Preserve repository-relative paths
Patch files must use their real repository-relative paths. SideScroll is currently a flat repo, so keep patch ZIPs flat unless the actual project structure changes.

## 5. Protect local authoring data
Preserve local game/editor/Design Lab data whenever possible. Do not recommend clearing site/PWA storage except as a genuine last resort. Prefer compatibility migrations, repair logic and fix-forward patches.

When the user provides a Complete Game Design/export JSON, use it as the best evidence of their current authored world state when debugging placement, puzzle or migration issues.

## 6. Design Lab merge rule — critical
Design Lab deliberately protects local edits. On load it merges **missing IDs** from the bundled `design-doc.json` into the working local document; it does **not** overwrite existing entries with the same ID.

Therefore, when a documentation update must reliably appear for an existing user without wiping their edits:
- add a new section/child with a new stable ID; or
- explicitly provide an import/reset migration if replacing existing content is truly required.

Merely changing the body/title of an existing bundled Design Lab ID may not appear in the user's existing working document.

## 7. PWA/service-worker caution
SideScroll is an offline PWA. Do not casually change cache names or create parallel cache strategies. Code/data should update cleanly online while retaining cached fallback offline. If a patch changes service-worker behaviour, say exactly what must be closed/reopened and test Safari plus the installed/A2HS copy when relevant.

## 8. Minimise blast radius
Prefer the smallest safe change set. Before adding a new system, identify ownership and data flow. Avoid duplicating authoritative state between scene editing, labs and runtime systems.

## 9. Current ownership model
- **Asset:** what an individual object is.
- **Puzzle:** how objects/rules combine into gameplay; puzzle-owned elements are relative to the puzzle marker.
- **World Element:** where authored content lives in the journey.
- **Section:** runtime/streaming chunk, not the primary creative authoring abstraction.

## 10. Current technical priority
The current priority is **world composition / World Lab**, not new puzzle authoring. Finish/verify Broken Bridge portability, formalise World Elements, then build World Lab before returning to Puzzle Lab unless a dependency changes that order.

children.title: Normal phone-first development loop
children.body:
1. Work from the latest known-good SideScroll baseline.
2. Discuss/design the next change in ChatGPT.
3. ChatGPT edits and validates only the files required for that change.
4. ChatGPT returns a **PATCH ZIP** containing only changed/new files.
5. On iPhone, unzip the patch in Files.
6. Upload those files to the root of the existing GitHub repository, replacing files with the same names.
7. Wait for GitHub Pages to publish, then test the live/PWA build.
8. Report the result. If the change passes, it becomes part of the working baseline; if not, fix forward or restore the prior Git version/full snapshot.

children.title: Patch releases — default
children.body:
Use a patch for normal code/data changes. A patch contains **only files that differ from the current baseline**.

Examples:
- Gameplay change: perhaps `sidescroll.js` only.
- Design Lab content: `design-doc.json` plus `sw.js` when cache refresh is required.
- New tool: its new HTML/JS/CSS files plus any existing navigation/service-worker files that genuinely changed.
- New artwork: only the new/replaced image files and any data/code that references them.

Do **not** include unchanged texture atlases, audio, character art or other large assets merely because they exist in the project.

The patch filename should identify the baseline/target or purpose clearly.

children.title: Full snapshot releases — safety checkpoints
children.body:
Keep occasional full flat ZIPs as known-good recovery points. Create a new full snapshot when a change is structurally significant, for example:
- Puzzle Lab / World Lab introduction
- major module/file reorganisation
- biome-system foundation
- save/data-schema migration
- substantial new asset library
- milestone/vertical-slice releases

Full snapshots are backups and release checkpoints; they are **not** required for every small iteration.

children.title: Uploading a patch to GitHub from iPhone
children.body:
## Patch upload
- Unzip the patch in the iOS Files app.
- The patch is flat: files are intended for the repository root unless a future patch explicitly contains folders.
- Upload every file in the patch to the existing SideScroll repository.
- When GitHub reports an existing filename, replace/update that file.
- Do not delete any repo files that are absent from the patch. Absence means **unchanged**, not removed.
- Commit the upload as one logical change where practical.

## After upload
Open the GitHub Pages build and verify the requested behaviour. For the installed PWA, a service-worker-changing patch may require closing/reopening once while the new cache activates.

children.title: Versioning, rollback & deletion rules
children.body:
## Versioning
- Small patch-only changes can sit on the current full-build baseline while being described by purpose/revision.
- Promote to a new numbered full SideScroll ZIP at meaningful checkpoints.
- Git history provides fine-grained revision history between full snapshots.

## Rollback
Preferred rollback order:
1. Revert the GitHub commit.
2. Restore specific files from the previous commit.
3. If necessary, restore the latest known-good full ZIP.

## Deletions
A patch that intentionally removes a project file must say so explicitly in the accompanying chat/release notes. Never infer deletion because a file is missing from a patch.

children.title: README rule — every patch carries the handoff
children.body:
Every changed-files-only patch must include an updated `README.md`, even when the functional change touched only one source file.

The README is the first-line handoff for a fresh conversation and should point future sessions toward **Design Lab → Project Workflow → READ FIRST — Assistant / Fresh-Chat Working Rules** for the full contract.

This keeps the repository self-describing rather than relying on cross-chat memory.

children.title: Patch packaging contract
children.body:
When producing a normal SideScroll patch:
- Include only changed or newly added project files.
- Keep repository-relative paths intact.
- Keep the project flat unless the real project structure changes.
- Identify any intentional deletions separately.
- Mention the required base/full version when compatibility depends on it.
- Include `sw.js` when the offline/PWA cache must be invalidated so new files/content reliably reach the installed app.
- Do not silently overwrite user-authored Design Lab working data; new bundled Design Lab sections should use the merge-safe ID system.
- Periodically create a complete numbered snapshot after major architectural milestones.

children.title: Current test — Workflow page patch
children.body:
[ ] Upload this patch containing only `design-doc.json` and `sw.js` over the existing v1.0.62 repository files.
[ ] Confirm GitHub Pages still loads normally.
[ ] Open Design Lab and confirm **Project Workflow** appears in the contents without losing existing local Design Lab edits.
[ ] Confirm Play, Asset Lab and Walk Lab still work without re-uploading any of their files.

If all four pass, changed-files-only patch delivery becomes the default SideScroll development workflow.

children.title: Patch workflow test result — adopted with safeguards
children.body:
The changed-files-only GitHub workflow is now adopted as the default.

The first test exposed two useful safeguards rather than invalidating the approach: avoid competing service-worker cache versions, and always ship an updated README. The recovery also confirmed that small targeted patches can restore the installed PWA without clearing local world/editor data.

**Current convention:** small patch ZIPs for normal work; periodic full ZIPs for safety/milestones.

sections.title: Technical Design & Development Queue
sections.body:
This is the implementation-facing companion to the story/design sections. It records the architectural and tooling work required to turn SideScroll into a longer, multi-biome game while protecting the phone-first workflow.

## How to use this section
Work broadly top-to-bottom because later items depend on earlier architecture. Check an item only when its “done means” behaviour works in the real game, not merely when code exists. Preserve useful implementation detail here so decisions do not disappear inside chat history.

## Current focus
Broken Bridge is the reference test for portable puzzle-owned world modification. Once that contract is proven, Puzzle Lab and the World Element/World Lab systems can build on it.

children.title: 01 — Broken Bridge owns its world modifiers
children.body:
[ ] Make Broken Bridge portable rather than dependent on a manually prepared River section.

**Implementation landed in v1.0.62; leave unchecked until the on-device move/delete/reload portability test passes.**

## Why first
This is the strongest existing test case for the boundary between Puzzle and World. Fallen Tree is self-contained; Broken Bridge requires the world underneath it to change. Solving this correctly defines the ownership model needed by later Puzzle Lab and World Lab work.

## Implemented in v1.0.62
- Broken Bridge gains a puzzle-owned `river` world modifier stored relative to its marker.
- Existing saved River-section width/position is migrated into that modifier on first load.
- The old absolute River section is released back to normal base terrain.
- River geometry, water, depth and collision gap move with the puzzle marker.
- The modifier can cross 10 m section boundaries; sections are runtime chunks rather than placement constraints.
- Removing the puzzle removes its river modifier automatically.
- Puzzle snapshots carry `worldModifiers` so linked/unique puzzle starts retain environmental requirements.

## Done means
Move the puzzle to several positions, including across a section boundary; its river follows. Delete the placed puzzle; the river disappears and underlying terrain returns. Reload/reset must not restore the old absolute River section.

children.title: 01A — River bank dressing & terrain grounding follow the puzzle modifier
children.body:
[ ] Verify on device that modifier-owned river-bank dressing, trees and nearby environment all resolve to the correct terrain height after moving Broken Bridge.

## Implemented in v1.0.62
- Broken Bridge river modifier now carries a deterministic `bankDressing` recipe rather than relying on section-owned auto-dressing.
- Legacy section-generated bridge bank dressing is removed during migration.
- Bank grasses/rocks are generated as puzzle-owned modifier dressing, stream with the puzzle, regenerate when it moves and disappear when it unloads/deletes.
- Procedural trees now anchor to `terrainGroundYAt(...)` instead of the old global `groundY`.
- Moving a puzzle re-anchors grounded puzzle props and nearby world dressing against the new terrain while preserving authored offsets.
- Non-puzzle dressing that falls inside a river channel is hidden rather than left embedded in the river bed.

## Done means
Move Broken Bridge through several positions and section boundaries. River-bank dressing follows; bank/nearby trees sit on the visible surface; nothing remains at the old river; no unrelated dressing changes height unexpectedly.

children.title: 02 — Formalise the puzzle ownership / world-modifier contract
children.body:
[ ] Generalise the bridge solution into a documented puzzle contract.

A puzzle may own objects, triggers, paths, respawn rules, thought nodes and world modifiers. Every owned element must be relative to the puzzle marker and disappear or move with its owner. External dependencies should be explicit requirements (for example “player must know Climb”), not hidden scene preparation.

## Done means
Every puzzle can report: owned objects, owned world modifiers, required abilities, and deliberate external dependencies. No puzzle silently relies on manually prepared section state.

children.title: CURRENT PRIORITY — World composition before Puzzle Lab
children.body:
The earlier queue placed Puzzle Lab immediately after puzzle ownership. Current design needs have changed: the next major authoring problem is **where the whole game is composed**, not how to invent another puzzle.

## Active order
[ ] Finish/verify Broken Bridge portability: puzzle objects + river/world modifier + bank dressing + terrain anchoring all move/delete/reload together.
[ ] Formalise the **World Element** data model and ownership rules.
[ ] Build **World Lab v1** as a second editing view over the same authoritative world data.
[ ] Add Biome Profiles, transition zones/blend curves, semantic dressing groups and bespoke dressing to that model.
[ ] Build the first Woodland → Mountain world transition and use it to drive climbing/environment development.
[ ] Return to **Puzzle Lab** once the world model it needs to test against is stable.

Puzzle Lab remains important; it is intentionally deferred, not cancelled.

children.title: 03 — Puzzle Lab v1
children.body:
[ ] Build a dedicated puzzle sandbox/test harness.

## Core v1
- Load one reusable puzzle in a disposable test world.
- Reset/Test/Set Start without disturbing the main game layout.
- Move the puzzle freely, including across section boundaries.
- Delete/recreate and stream out/in.
- Visualise bounds, owned objects, triggers, collision, paths and world modifiers.
- Show external dependencies.
- Environment selector initially: Blank/Test and Woodland; later Mountain/Wetlands.

## Portability test
Centre of section → boundary → arbitrary offset → reload → delete → recreate. Broken Bridge is the first acceptance puzzle.

children.title: 04 — World Element data model & ownership
children.body:
[ ] Define one common representation for intentionally authored world content.

Candidate element types: Puzzle, Biome Region, Biome Transition, Dressing Group, Explicit Dressing, Artefact/Landmark, Story Trigger, Audio Zone, VFX Zone, Spawn/Checkpoint.

Common data should include world position/range, extent, owner, streaming policy, links and optional biome response.

## Principle
World Elements are how we author the journey; 10 m Sections are how the engine streams/renders it.

children.title: World Element v1 — proposed common schema
children.body:
World Elements are the authored placement layer that World Lab and in-scene Edit Mode both manipulate.

## Initial element types
- Puzzle Instance
- Biome Region
- Biome Transition
- Semantic Dressing Group
- Explicit/Bespoke Dressing
- Terraform Machine / Landmark
- Story Trigger
- Camera Sequence Node
- Audio Zone / Emitter
- VFX / Anomaly Zone
- Spawn / Checkpoint

## Common fields
- stable ID / type / template reference;
- world X (and Z/Y or range/volume when needed);
- extent: point, range or volume;
- owner and parent links;
- streaming/load policy;
- links to related elements;
- optional biome-aware behaviour;
- authored/runtime state separated cleanly.

## Rule
World Lab and scene Edit Mode edit **the same data**. Neither may maintain a second copy of placement state.

children.title: 05 — World Lab v1
children.body:
[ ] Create the horizontal whole-journey authoring view.

## v1 tracks
- Section boundaries (optional/debug).
- Puzzle markers.
- Biome regions / transitions.
- Bespoke dressing and dressing groups.

Placement must be bidirectional: moving a puzzle/object in the scene moves its World Lab marker; dragging its marker in World Lab moves the real game object. Both views edit the same data, never duplicated copies.

Later tracks: story beats, artefacts, checkpoints, audio/VFX and pacing diagnostics.

children.title: World Lab v1 — implementation scope
children.body:
## Core view
A horizontally scrollable/zoomable representation of the playable journey measured in world distance. It should show authored components as tracks/markers rather than trying to render the 3D scene.

## v1 tracks
1. **Biome regions / transitions** — ranges with draggable start/end handles and later blend-curve controls.
2. **Puzzles** — marker plus optional extent; drag to reposition the real puzzle instance.
3. **Dressing** — bespoke objects and semantic dressing-group ranges/markers.
4. **Terraform machines / landmarks** — major world anchors.
5. Optional/debug **section boundaries** so runtime chunks remain visible without becoming the authoring model.

## Bidirectional editing
- Place/move a puzzle or dressing item in the scene → World Lab marker updates.
- Drag/move it in World Lab → scene/game placement updates.
- Both operate on the same World Element ID/data.

## Selection panel
Tapping an element should expose type, position/range, owner, biome response, links/dependencies and actions such as **Jump to Game**, duplicate/delete and eventually **Open in Puzzle Lab / Asset Lab / Design Lab**.

## Later tracks
Story beats, camera nodes, audio/VFX zones, checkpoints and pacing diagnostics can be layered in after the placement model is proven.

children.title: 06 — Biome Profile system
children.body:
[ ] Turn “Woodland”, “Mountain”, “Wetlands” etc. into data profiles rather than hard-coded scenery modes.

A profile can define terrain/ground materials, tree/rock/plant libraries, density tendencies, foreground/background dressing, fog/grade, ambient audio, weather/VFX and biome-specific semantic dressing mappings.

Start with Woodland (existing) plus Mountain (new).

children.title: 07 — Biome transition zones & blend curves
children.body:
[ ] Allow a continuous journey from one biome to another.

Author a transition with FROM biome, TO biome, start position/section, end position/section and blend curve. The engine samples blend weights by world position. Support Linear / Smooth / Early / Late initially, with custom curve later.

Blend more than object spawn percentages: terrain dressing, density, fog/grade, ambient audio, VFX and distant silhouettes should be able to transition too.

children.title: 08 — Biome-aware dressing groups + bespoke dressing
children.body:
[ ] Add semantic dressing groups where the designer places an intent rather than one fixed asset.

Examples: Dense Edge, Sparse Edge, Ground Detail, Path Breakup, Foreground Occluder, Background Mass, Rock Cluster, Vegetation Cluster, Artefact Disturbance.

Woodland may realise Dense Edge as trees/ferns; Mountain as rock wall/boulders/scrub; Wetlands as reeds/willow/water plants.

Keep explicit bespoke placement alongside this for exact hero objects and composition.

children.title: 09 — Mountain biome content pack & first full environment transition
children.body:
[ ] Build enough Mountain content to prove the world can genuinely change environment.

Minimum set: large rock/cliff forms, smaller rock clusters/scree, mountain grasses/scrub, sparse tree variants and distant mountain silhouettes.

Acceptance target: walk continuously from established Woodland through a blended transition into a recognisably Mountain environment without a hard scene cut.

children.title: 10 — Climbing movement & traversal system
children.body:
[ ] Introduce Climb as the next major traversal mechanic, strongly associated with mountain progression but reusable elsewhere.

Target vocabulary: grab, hang, shimmy, climb up, drop and jump from ledge; possibly vertical climb surfaces later. Use a clear authored visual/gameplay language rather than making every surface climbable.

Climbing should create puzzle possibilities, not turn the game into a twitch platformer.

children.title: 10A — Cutscene Camera / Camera Sequence Nodes
children.body:
[ ] Add lightweight authored camera overrides for story beats, reveals and environmental emphasis.

## Design intent
Use a Thought-Node-like placed trigger rather than a heavyweight cutscene editor. The normal follow camera remains the default; a Camera Sequence Node temporarily takes ownership, performs a short authored move/hold, then hands control back smoothly.

## Camera Sequence Node v1
- Trigger position/range and optional approach direction.
- Target may be a fixed world point or a linked world object/puzzle element.
- Ease/pan time into the override.
- Hold duration at the target.
- Optional follow-target behaviour during the hold.
- Optional player movement/input lock while the sequence owns the camera.
- Smooth return/ease time back to the normal player-follow camera.
- One-shot, resettable or repeatable trigger behaviour.
- Optional chaining later for simple multi-shot sequences.

## Example uses
- Broken bridge: briefly look over the gap so the player cannot miss the obstacle/solution space.
- Aureli opening: temporarily prevent the player leaving while the silence/deer/Darkness sequence is staged.
- Artefact reveals: pan or hold on a machine as it wakes or changes the environment.

## Ownership / world integration
Camera Sequence Nodes should become World Elements and may be owned by the World, a Story beat or a Puzzle. If an owning puzzle moves, its linked camera target/trigger must move with it.

## Done means
Place a node in-world, trigger it from either direction as configured, ease to a target, optionally lock movement, hold, and return to follow-camera without a visible snap. Moving/deleting its owner also moves/deletes the node.

children.title: 11 — Walk Lab → Anim Lab
children.body:
[ ] Expand Walk Lab into a general character/creature animation tool without discarding the existing rig work.

Characters: Aureli, fox, boy and future NPCs. Actions can grow from Idle/Walk/Run/Jump into Carry, Push, Pull, Climb, Hang, Shimmy, Swim, Dive, Interact and companion-specific actions.

Longer-term controls: rig/atlas selection, action preview, loop/speed, contact lines/targets and transition testing.

children.title: 12 — Terraforming-machine biome framework
children.body:
[ ] Define how major terraforming machines belong visually and mechanically to their biome.

First pair:
- Woodland biological/biosphere machine: ancient tree integration, bio-mechanical vines/light, plant/animal seeding and transformation. Supports the fox/boy transformation logic.
- Mountain geophysical/gravity machine: integrated into rock/mountain mass, gravity and tectonic/topographic control. Supports gravity anomalies and mountain formation.

Each machine should have: original terraforming job, centuries/millennia of environmental integration, anomaly/failure behaviour, visual language and puzzle powers.

children.title: 13 — Concept Lab v1
children.body:
[ ] Create the project visual-development library.

Organise concepts by World/Biome/Artefact/Character/Location. Store image, prompt, notes, status, version/date and links back to Design Lab. Support multiple iterations and an Approved Direction state.

Initial implementation should prioritise image import/organisation and prompt history. Do not expose an AI API key in the static GitHub Pages client; integrated generation can later use a protected backend or generation through ChatGPT followed by import.

children.title: 14 — Wetlands / hydrology biome + swimming/diving exploration
children.body:
[ ] Develop a later biome around the hydrological terraforming system.

Environment: wetlands, deeper water, reeds/mud/aquatic life and an underwater major machine. Original responsibilities may include water creation/distribution, salinity, groundwater/rain cycles, temperature and aquatic ecosystems.

Potential movement expansion: swimming/diving, buoyancy/current interactions and underwater puzzle spaces. Build only after the biome/world foundations and climbing/animation pipeline are stable.

sections.title: Technical Roadmap
sections.body: Technical work should protect iteration speed and be pulled by actual game needs.

children.title: Phase A — Production-ready opening
children.body:
- Protect the direct browser/GitHub Pages workflow.
- Modularise the largest systems safely.
- Formalise chapter/level manifest data.
- Move unique scenery toward section ownership/spatial indexing.
- Add a save abstraction.
- Use the first 20–30 minutes to expose missing production systems.

children.title: Phase B — Richer world systems
children.body:
- Asset lifecycle / preloading and release.
- Reusable pooled VFX emitters.
- Expanded post stack with quality scaling.
- SFX mixer, ambience and local emitters.
- Narrative encounter framework when story requires it.
- Generalised puzzle completion/state graph.

children.title: Phase C — Multi-hour production
children.body:
- Checkpoints, Continue, save slots and migrations.
- Draw-call / texture-memory profiling and batching where density requires it.
- Reset/save/reload QA habits for puzzle state and chapter transitions.
- Keyboard/controller abstraction.
- Player-facing settings and accessibility options.

children.title: Phase D — Store-ready packaging
children.body: Keep gameplay code common. Wrap the finished web-native game for iOS/Android and desktop, add platform signing/store metadata and optional native services without forking gameplay logic.

sections.title: Platform & Store Readiness
sections.body:
Native packaging is a later distribution layer, not a reason to rewrite the game.

- **iPhone / iPad:** Capacitor/native WebView wrapper. Prepare orientation/lifecycle abstraction, safe storage and optional haptics/Game Center later.
- **Android:** Capacitor/native WebView wrapper with Android packaging/signing and device QA.
- **Windows / Steam:** Electron initially for a predictable bundled Chromium runtime; add keyboard/controller, fullscreen/window handling and desktop save/cloud adapter.
- **macOS/Linux:** potential Electron/Tauri packaging after the desktop game is proven.

Over time gameplay code should call small SideScroll services rather than browser APIs directly: Save, Audio, Input, Orientation/Fullscreen, Haptics, Achievements/Platform and File/Cloud storage.

sections.title: Open Design Questions
sections.body:
## Priority 1 — story spine
- Who is the protagonist: name, age, home, personality and key relationship?
- Why does she leave, and what destination does she initially believe she is trying to reach?
- What is the central mystery or truth of the world?
- What emotional change should the player feel in her by the ending?

## Priority 2 — structure and tone
- Is the game one continuous physical journey, chapter-based loads, or a hybrid?
- How unsettling, sad or frightening can the world become?
- What is the role of other characters: rare encounters, recurring companion, settlement inhabitants, memories, or something else?
- What does the Stone Wall / Forest Key thread lead to?

## Priority 3 — production shape
- Which 5–8 mechanics form the full game’s reusable core vocabulary?
- What environmental families make 2–4 hours feel rich without unsustainable bespoke art?
- What is Chapter 1’s final story beat that makes the player want to continue?

## Recommended next design exercise
Write the one-paragraph premise and protagonist bio first, then outline the five chapter story beats in only one or two sentences each. Once that spine exists, map current/future puzzles onto it and identify where new mechanics are truly needed.

children.title: Hidden Canon — Decisions Still Open
children.body:
- Why did the intended colonists not arrive as expected?
- What is the true origin of Aureli's people?
- What triggered the current large-scale correction?
- Is the network sentient, emergent, or merely adaptive?
- What exactly happens to organisms inside the Darkness?
- What determines a transformed organism's new form?
- Can transformation be deliberately reversed or controlled?
- What local / global consequence would follow if the network were stopped?
- Does the civilisation that launched the missions still exist?
- Which truths, if any, should Game 1 reveal explicitly?## Ending / Darkness questions added in v0.4
- Why does the Darkness collect living things: targeted biological maintenance, incidental regional processing, or both?
- Which systems are capable of recognising the intended colonists, and is that ability deliberately restricted to the central interface?
- Does Aureli satisfy the arrival check because her species is already compatible, because the journey changes her, or through a combination of both?
- What exact phrase / concept does the machine apply to Aureli: creator, colonist, authorised user, compatible arrival, or something less explicit?
- How does the father return / resolve once the correction is suspended?
- Does maintenance mode reverse any transformations, merely stop new ones, or allow particular systems to stabilise them?
- How much of the central interface should the player be able to interpret directly?
